newsitem.title: UK: UK shares tumble for second day amid Dow jitters.
newsitem.headline: UK shares tumble for second day amid Dow jitters.

text.p: ** FTSE 100 drops over 70 points for second day as jittery
Wall Street prompts profit-taking after recent peaks.
Dealers say underlying trend still firm.
** BT drops on fears for MCI alliance, Utd Utilities hit by
ceo departure. Pru tumbles as NatWest merger hopes fade.
"There is some profit-taking but it is not a panic," said the head of equity trading at one U.S. investment bank. "The trend is still holding up and I would expect it to resume some time soon."
UK shares were led lower from the outset by a sharp fall on Wall Street on Friday. Yet the Dow had recovered from an early 50-point loss by London's close on Monday, to be up some 9.5 points.
With no sign yet of a sustained pickup in inflation on either side of the Atlantic, dealers said the steady flow of investment cash into stocks should continue.

"The bears are out in force because they have never seen the market this high, but wait till it goes through 6,000," said another head of equity trading. "I don't see any selling and there is enough money out there to buy on the falls."

Yet one potential negative for shares came in a Sunday newspaper report that raised the possibility of a recession next year if interest rates went on rising as the Bank of England attempts to prevent the economy overheating.
Dealers noted that rising rates had not proved a negative for shares so far but could weigh on them if seen taking a significant toll on company profits.
Meantime, dealers said recent Wall Street volatility had led to concern that equity markets were due a sharp correction.
A report in U.S. investment newspaper Barron's, for instance, drew parallels between the recent bull run in equities and the situation at the time of stock market crashes in 1929 and 1987.
Yet dealers played down the current bout of market unease.

"At this stage I can't get too bearish," said the head of equity sales at one top brokerage, "because not much has changed on the inflation and interest rate outlook...any setback at the moment is going to be a short, sharp shock but not much more than that."
Markets were also cautious ahead of Tuesday's set piece Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on the state of the U.S. economy by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan.
Participants were mindfull of Greenspan's warning last December of "irrational exuberance" on Wall Street, but said there were few major clouds on the horizon for the U.S. economy.
Anyway, the Fed chief has commented since last year that he had no intention of trying to prick a stock market bubble with higher short-term interest rates.
Other UK indexes also fell, with the FTSE 250 index of mid-range stocks down 20.0 points at 4,464.1.
The FT-Actuaries All-Share index, the broadest measure of the UK market, dropped 27.65 points or 1.2 percent at 2,256.49.
Trading volume was a robust 1.3 billion shares by 1609 GMT but much of that total was accounted for by 689 million Thorn shares after the company bought back all its B shares at 20-1/4p.
British Telecom was the most active stock in the FTSE 100 amid continued fears over prospects of its planned merger with MCI. Its shares fell 15-1/2p to 414-1/2p in volume of 34 million shares.
United Utilities was the biggest decliner in the FTSE 100, down 67p or 8.7 percent to 702, after announcing the departure of its chief executive.

Banks, meanwhile, fell sharply as profit-taking set in after recent gains. Barclays fell 45p to 12.38 stg, Alliance & Leicester dropped 22-1/2p to 840, Halifax declined 15-1/2p to 735-1/2 and Lloyds TSB fell 18-1/2p to 658-1/2.
Prudential fell 26-1/2p to 559-1/2 as hopes faded for a merger with NatWest, down 6-1/2p to 860.
Prize for the biggest gainer in the FTSE went to Commercial Union, up 11p to 694-1/2 amid vague talk of a bid from ABN AMRO .
-- David Holmes, London Newsroom +44 17 1542 4367
